claim: The FTC says its Health Breach Notification Rule "applies to most health apps that aren't covered by HIPAA".
quote: The FTC’s Health Breach Notification Rule applies to most health apps that aren’t covered by HIPAA because most developers of health apps are acting as “health care providers”

claim: The rule is 16 CFR part 318.
quote: 16 CFR Part 318: Health Breach Notification Rule

claim: Section 318.1 says the rule "applies to foreign and domestic vendors of personal health records, PHR related entities, and third party service providers, irrespective of any jurisdictional tests in the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Act, that maintain information of U.S. citizens or residents."
quote: This part applies to foreign and domestic vendors of personal health records, PHR related entities, and third party service providers, irrespective of any jurisdictional tests in the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Act, that maintain information of U.S. citizens or residents.

claim: It "does not apply to HIPAA-covered entities, or to any other entity to the extent that it engages in activities as a business associate of a HIPAA-covered entity."
quote: This part does not apply to HIPAA-covered entities, or to any other entity to the extent that it engages in activities as a business associate of a HIPAA-covered entity.

claim: Vendor of personal health records: an entity, other than a HIPAA-covered entity or business associate, that offers or maintains a personal health record.
quote: Vendor of personal health records means an entity, other than a HIPAA-covered entity or an entity to the extent that it engages in activities as a business associate of a HIPAA-covered entity, that offers or maintains a personal health record.

claim: FTC example of a vendor: a health app that collects information from consumers and can sync with a consumer's fitness tracker.
quote: For example, if you develop a health app that collects information from consumers and can sync with a consumer’s fitness tracker, you’re probably a vendor of personal health records.

claim: PHR related entity: offers products or services through a personal health record vendor's website or online service, or accesses or sends unsecured health information in a personal health record.
quote: Offers products or services through the website, including any online service, of a vendor of personal health records;

claim: PHR related entity: accesses or sends unsecured health information in a personal health record.
quote: Accesses unsecured PHR identifiable health information in a personal health record or sends unsecured PHR identifiable health information to a personal health record.

claim: FTC example of a PHR related entity: a company that offers a fitness tracker and sends identifiable health information to health apps.
quote: For example, a company that offers a fitness tracker is likely a PHR related entity if it sends identifiable health information to health apps

claim: Third party service provider: provides services to a vendor or related entity and, as a result, holds, uses or discloses unsecured health information.
quote: Accesses, maintains, retains, modifies, records, stores, destroys, or otherwise holds, uses, or discloses unsecured PHR identifiable health information as a result of such services.

claim: FTC example of a third party service provider: a company a vendor hires for billing, debt collection or data storage related to health information.
quote: For example, if a vendor of personal health records hires your company to provide billing, debt collection, or data storage services related to health information, you’re a third party service provider, and covered by the Rule.

claim: A personal health record is "an electronic record of PHR identifiable health information on an individual that has the technical capacity to draw information from multiple sources and that is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual."
quote: Personal health record (PHR) means an electronic record of PHR identifiable health information on an individual that has the technical capacity to draw information from multiple sources and that is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual.

claim: The FTC's guide gives a diet app where users enter daily weights and an API pulls calorie counts from restaurant menus as a case where "there's a good chance you have a PHR covered by the FTC's Rule."
quote: let’s say a diet app that allows users to enter daily weights and an API for pulling calorie counts from restaurant menus – there’s a good chance you have a PHR covered by the FTC’s Rule.

claim: The protected information must be created or received by, among others, a covered health care provider.
quote: Is created or received by a:

claim: A covered health care provider includes "any other entity furnishing health care services or supplies."
quote: or any other entity furnishing health care services or supplies.

claim: Health care services or supplies means "any online service such as a website, mobile application, or internet-connected device that provides mechanisms to track ... fitness, fertility, sexual health, sleep, mental health, genetic information, diet, or that provides other health-related services or tools."
quote: Health care services or supplies means any online service such as a website, mobile application, or internet-connected device that provides mechanisms to track diseases, health conditions, diagnoses or diagnostic testing, treatment, medications, vital signs, symptoms, bodily functions, fitness, fertility, sexual health, sleep, mental health, genetic information, diet, or that provides other health-related services or tools.

claim: The FTC's tool: the July 2024 amendments "explain that most health app developers act as 'covered health care providers' when they furnish health care services or supplies – in this case, their app – to consumers."
quote: July 2024 amendments to the Health Breach Notification Rule explain that most health app developers act as “covered health care providers” when they furnish health care services or supplies – in this case, their app – to consumers.

claim: Asked about an app where users enter their height, weight and age, which can sync with wearable fitness trackers that only some users connect...
quote: My company makes a fitness app, in which consumers input their height, weight, age, and other information. The app, which consumers can download from the app store, can sync with wearable fitness trackers. Some of our users use this syncing feature, but others don’t.

claim: ...the FTC replies: "You are likely a vendor of personal health records."
quote: You are likely a vendor of personal health records. Your app includes identifiable health information, such as consumers’ names, weight, height, age, and steps taken.

claim: The app has the technical capacity to draw identifiable health information from both the consumer and the tracker, "even if some consumers choose to not connect the fitness tracker."
quote: even if some consumers choose to not connect the fitness tracker.

claim: The rule defines a breach of security as the "acquisition of such information without the authorization of the individual."
quote: Breach of security means, with respect to unsecured PHR identifiable health information of an individual in a personal health record, acquisition of such information without the authorization of the individual.

claim: It presumes unauthorized access is acquisition unless the company "has reliable evidence showing that there has not been, or could not reasonably have been, unauthorized acquisition of such information".
quote: Unauthorized acquisition will be presumed to include unauthorized access to unsecured PHR identifiable health information unless the vendor of personal health records, PHR related entity, or third party service provider that experienced the breach has reliable evidence showing that there has not been, or could not reasonably have been, unauthorized acquisition of such information.

claim: A breach includes an unauthorized acquisition "that occurs as a result of a data breach or an unauthorized disclosure."
quote: A breach of security includes an unauthorized acquisition of unsecured PHR identifiable health information in a personal health record that occurs as a result of a data breach or an unauthorized disclosure.

claim: The FTC's guide says "if you disclose consumers' unsecured, individually identifiable health information without their consent, a breach has occurred."
quote: if you disclose consumers’ unsecured, individually identifiable health information without their consent, a breach has occurred.

claim: Its example: a company that shares "your users' medical information along with their mobile identifiers with an ad network for the purpose of targeted marketing without first getting the person's consent."
quote: suppose you share your users’ medical information along with their mobile identifiers with an ad network for the purpose of targeted marketing without first getting the person’s consent.

claim: No names were shared in that example, and the FTC says the information "could still readily identify individual consumers".
quote: Names weren’t disclosed in either example. But the information disclosed could still readily identify individual consumers, so it counts as PHR identifiable health information.

claim: The rule covers information not protected by a technology or methodology that HHS specifies.
quote: Unsecured means PHR identifiable information that is not protected through the use of a technology or methodology specified by the Secretary of Health and Human Services

claim: The FTC's guide says HHS's definition includes "any information that is not encrypted or destroyed", and that losing a laptop holding only encrypted personal health records would not require notice.
quote: defined by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to include any information that is not encrypted or destroyed. For example, if your employee loses a laptop containing only encrypted personal health records, you wouldn’t be required to notify people.

claim: "If your business experiences a breach involving only paper health records – not electronic records – the FTC's Rule doesn't require any notification."
quote: If your business experiences a breach involving only paper health records – not electronic records – the FTC’s Rule doesn’t require any notification.

claim: A breach counts as discovered "as of the first day on which such breach is known or reasonably should have been known".
quote: A breach of security shall be treated as discovered as of the first day on which such breach is known or reasonably should have been known to the vendor of personal health records, PHR related entity, or third party service provider, respectively.

claim: Including when it is known to any employee, officer or other agent other than the person who committed it.
quote: to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is an employee, officer, or other agent of such vendor of personal health records, PHR related entity, or third party service provider.

claim: Each affected U.S. citizen or resident must be notified.
quote: Notify each individual who is a citizen or resident of the United States whose unsecured PHR identifiable health information was acquired by an unauthorized person as a result of such breach of security;

claim: Without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery.
quote: shall be sent without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after the discovery of a breach of security.

claim: The FTC, when 500 or more people are affected: at the same time as the notices to individuals.
quote: involving the unsecured PHR identifiable health information of 500 or more individuals shall be provided contemporaneously with the notice required by paragraph (a) of this section.

claim: The FTC, when fewer than 500 people are affected: may be logged and sent once a year, no later than 60 calendar days after the calendar year ends.
quote: involving the unsecured PHR identifiable health information of fewer than 500 individuals may be sent annually to the Federal Trade Commission no later than 60 calendar days following the end of the calendar year.

claim: Prominent media outlets in a state or jurisdiction, when 500 or more of its residents are affected.
quote: Notify prominent media outlets serving a State or jurisdiction, following the discovery of a breach of security, if the unsecured PHR identifiable health information of 500 or more residents of such State or jurisdiction is, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired during such breach.

claim: A third party service provider notifies the official the contract names, or else a senior official, with acknowledgment that it was received.
quote: provide notice of the breach to an official designated in a written contract by the vendor of personal health records or the PHR related entity to receive such notices or, if such a designation is not made, to a senior official at the vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity to which it provides services, and obtain acknowledgment from such official that such notice was received.

claim: The FTC's guide says that if a company gathers the necessary information within 30 days, "it would be unreasonable to wait until the 60th day" to notify people.
quote: That means if a company discovers a breach and gathers the necessary information within, say, 30 days, it would be unreasonable to wait until the 60th day to notify the people whose information was breached.

claim: A law enforcement official can delay notice that "would impede a criminal investigation or cause damage to national security".
quote: If a law enforcement official determines that a notification, notice, or posting required under this part would impede a criminal investigation or cause damage to national security, such notification, notice, or posting shall be delayed.

claim: The company carries "the burden of demonstrating that all notifications were made as required under this part".
quote: shall have the burden of demonstrating that all notifications were made as required under this part, including evidence demonstrating the necessity of any delay.

claim: Notice to the FTC goes through its online form, the Notice of Breach of Health Information.
quote: To report the breach to the agency, you must use the following online form: Notice of Breach of Health Information

claim: Written notice goes to the individual's last known address, and may go by electronic mail if the individual has chosen that as the primary method.
quote: Written notice at the last known address of the individual. Written notice may be sent by electronic mail if the individual has specified electronic mail as the primary method of communication.

claim: The rule defines electronic mail as "email in combination with one or more of the following: text message, within-application messaging, or electronic banner".
quote: Electronic mail means email in combination with one or more of the following: text message, within-application messaging, or electronic banner.

claim: If contact details are insufficient or out of date for ten or more people, the rule requires substitute notice.
quote: finds that contact information for ten or more individuals is insufficient or out-of-date, the vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity shall provide substitute notice

claim: Substitute notice: a conspicuous posting on the website's home page for 90 days, or notice in major print or broadcast media.
quote: Through a conspicuous posting for a period of 90 days on the home page of its website; or

claim: Each with a toll-free number that stays active for at least 90 days.
quote: Such a notice in media or web posting shall include a toll-free phone number, which shall remain active for at least 90 days

claim: Section 318.6 sets the content, in plain language.
quote: notice of a breach of security shall be in plain language and include, to the extent possible, the following:

claim: What happened, including the dates of the breach and of its discovery if known, and the identity of any third parties that acquired the information.
quote: A brief description of what happened, including: the date of the breach and the date of the discovery of the breach, if known; and the full name or identity

claim: The types of information involved, a list that names "the individual's use of a health-related mobile application" and a "device identifier (in combination with another data element)".
quote: the individual's use of a health-related mobile application, or device identifier (in combination with another data element)

claim: Steps individuals should take to protect themselves.
quote: Steps individuals should take to protect themselves from potential harm resulting from the breach;

claim: What the company is doing to investigate, mitigate harm and protect against further breaches.
quote: A brief description of what the entity that experienced the breach is doing to investigate the breach, to mitigate harm, to protect against any further breaches, and to protect affected individuals

claim: At least two ways to make contact, chosen from a toll-free telephone number, email address, website, within-application, or postal address.
quote: which must include two or more of the following: toll-free telephone number; email address; website; within-application; or postal address.

claim: Section 318.7 treats a violation as a violation of an FTC rule on unfair or deceptive acts or practices, subject to civil penalties as adjusted for inflation.
quote: regarding unfair or deceptive acts or practices, and thus subject to civil penalties (as adjusted for inflation pursuant to

claim: The FTC's guide, edited in January 2025 to reflect inflation-adjusted maximums...
quote: Edited January 2025 to reflect Inflation-Adjusted Civil Penalty Maximums

claim: ...says businesses that violate the rule "may be subject to a civil penalty of up to $53,088 per violation."
quote: Businesses that violate the Rule may be subject to a civil penalty of up to $53,088 per violation.

claim: The FTC says a company that acts solely as a HIPAA business associate is outside the rule, and its duties sit in HHS's Breach Notification Rule.
quote: If you are a HIPAA-covered entity or act only as a HIPAA business associate, your responsibilities are in the Health and Human Services (HHS) Breach Notification Rule

claim: A business associate that also offers personal health record services to the public "may be subject to both the HHS and FTC Breach Notification Rules."
quote: If your company is a HIPAA business associate that also offers personal health record services to the public, you may be subject to both the HHS and FTC Breach Notification Rules.

claim: The FTC's rule "preempts contradictory state breach notification laws, but not those that impose additional – but non-contradictory – breach notification requirements".
quote: The FTC’s Rule preempts contradictory state breach notification laws, but not those that impose additional – but non-contradictory – breach notification requirements.

claim: The FTC says one notice can carry both sets of content.
quote: you could comply with both federal and state requirements by including all the information in a single breach notice.

claim: eCFR's current text records the rule as amended at 89 FR 47054 on May 30, 2024, and lists no later amendment.
quote: 74 FR 42980 , Aug. 25, 2009, as amended at 89 FR 47054 , May 30, 2024, unless otherwise noted.

claim: The FTC's guide says the "July 2024 amendments make clear that makers of health apps, connected devices, and similar products must comply with the Rule."
quote: July 2024 amendments make clear that makers of health apps, connected devices, and similar products must comply with the Rule.

claim: On September 9, 2026, the FTC rescinded its 2021 Policy Statement on Breaches by Health Apps and Other Connected Devices.
quote: The Federal Trade Commission rescinded the 2021 Policy Statement on Breaches by Health Apps and Other Connected Devices.

claim: The press release is dated September 9, 2026.
quote: FTC Withdraws Obsolete Policy Statement (September 9, 2026)

claim: The FTC said its 2024 update to the rule already covers "health apps and connected devices like fitness trackers, rendering the policy statement unnecessary."
quote: In 2024, however, the Commission updated the Health Breach Notification Rule to cover health apps and connected devices like fitness trackers, rendering the policy statement unnecessary.

claim: The FTC's tool asks which APIs you use, whether your app syncs with other health or fitness apps, and whether users can upload data from other sources or send it elsewhere.
quote: What application programing interfaces (APIs) do you use? Does your app sync with other health, wellness, diet, fitness, or other apps?

claim: ...whether users can upload data from other sources or send it elsewhere...
quote: Does your app allow users to upload data from other sources or send data from your app elsewhere?

claim: ...and says whether the rule applies "may depend on the answers to these questions".
quote: Whether the Rule applies may depend on the answers to these questions, so take some time to make sure you understand your data flows.

claim: The FTC's guide suggests finding out in advance, "perhaps when they sign up for your service", whether people prefer email or first-class mail.
quote: The best practice for notifying people is to find out from your customers in advance – perhaps when they sign up for your service – if they’d prefer to hear about a security breach by email or by first-class mail.

claim: An email plan needs a text, in-app or banner channel alongside it.
quote: If you’re notifying people by email, you must also notify people:

claim: The rule requires vendors and related entities to tell their third party service providers that they are covered.
quote: vendors of personal health records and PHR related entities shall notify third party service providers of their status as vendors of personal health records or PHR related entities subject to this part.
